cells.quote: Similarly, Alghabban & Hendley [74] found that adapting learning material to match both the dyslexia type and reading skill level of Arabic learners with dyslexia resulted in significantly better learning outcomes compared to providing non-adapted standard material—a pattern consistent with the importance of matching material difficulty to learners’ current abilities and specific learning needs.
cells.note: The study text does not report a printed effect size or design details.

O.outcome_detail: learning after reduced item exposure

cells.quote: Parallel findings have been observed in other domains: McGraw Fisher et al.[75] reported that reducing item exposure enhanced learning in typical readers but not in learners with dyslexia, and Pavlidou & Williams [76] found that higher-order rule learning tasks impaired performance in dyslexic learners while benefiting typical ones.
cells.note: The sentence reports the item-exposure contrast but does not provide a printed effect size or design details.

O.outcome_detail: performance on higher-order rule-learning tasks

cells.quote: Parallel findings have been observed in other domains: McGraw Fisher et al.[75] reported that reducing item exposure enhanced learning in typical readers but not in learners with dyslexia, and Pavlidou & Williams [76] found that higher-order rule learning tasks impaired performance in dyslexic learners while benefiting typical ones.
cells.note: The sentence reports the rule-learning contrast but does not provide a printed effect size or design details.

O.outcome_detail: artificial-script syllable reading

cells.quote: The results revealed that the DD group scored significantly lower than the TR group on each of the Syllable, Letter, and Word reading tasks (all ts > 2.10, all ps < .05).
cells.note: The study reports no printed effect size for this group contrast.

O.outcome_detail: visual symbol recognition

cells.quote: No significant differences were observed between the two groups on the more basic visual symbol recognition task (Posttest Visual).
cells.note: The non-significant result is inconclusive because no equivalence test or adequate-power claim is reported.

O.outcome_detail: performance on the UCSF Mathematical Cognition Battery

cells.quote: In summary, among the 75 participants referred with a diagnosis of dyslexia, 50 had trouble in mathematics (i.e., two-thirds of dyslexia sample). The clinician ’s assessment was con ﬁrmed for all but three (n = 47) of the children in the dyslexia group.
cells.note: The study reports clinically defined learner groups rather than randomized conditions.

D.comparison: other dyslexia and typically developing groups

O.outcome_detail: number-processing subtests

cells.quote: Children with deﬁcits in number processing (n = 10, 13.3% of dyslexia sample) performed signiﬁcantly lower than all other groups on number subtests and obtained low scores in most of the MCB ’s subtests.
cells.note: Groups were classified by clinicians and evaluated with the MCB.

D.comparison: other dyslexia and typically developing groups

O.outcome_detail: calculation accuracy and completion time

cells.quote: Notably, they performed signiﬁcantly differently from all other groups on the subtraction subtest: the completion time is the highest of all groups, and the performance is lower than the other groups, except for those with deﬁcits in number processing.
cells.note: The comparison is observational and the groups were not randomly assigned.

D.comparison: other dyslexia and typically developing groups

O.outcome_detail: multiplication and written-calculation performance

cells.quote: Children with deﬁcits in arithmetic facts retrieval ( n = 15, 20% of dyslexia sample) obtained low scoresor accurate but slow performance on multiplication and division problems (Supplementary Table 1: #11. Mental multiplication and #13. Written Calculation). They demonstrated a speciﬁc deﬁcit in the time to complete the multiplication table (see Supplementary Table 2 for inclusion and exclusion criteria). They also took the longest to complete the written calculation subtest, which also includes multiplication and division.
cells.note: This is a clinically defined subgroup comparison; the study does not report random assignment.

O.outcome_detail: relationship between reading performance and left SLF fractional anisotropy

cells.quote: Groups, however, did not differ in the correlations of reading and diffusion parameters – in both children with dyslexia and controls, reading was positively correlated with FA in the left SLF and phonological decoding was negatively correlated with MD in the corona radiata 52.
cells.note: The review interprets the shared positive reading–FA association as suggesting delayed rather than altered white-matter development in dyslexia.

O.outcome_detail: reading-network activation and hemispheric lateralization during reading

cells.quote: Children at risk of dyslexia aged 5–6 years hypoactivated the reading network at the early stage of reading training. Three months later, after intensive reading instruction, they showed bilateral temporo-parietal and frontal activity for words, while the control group employed left-lateralized temporo-parietal regions54.
cells.note: Narrative review of longitudinal neuroimaging studies; the reported pattern changes across time rather than showing a single direction.

O.outcome_detail: left ventral occipito-temporal and inferior frontal activation during implicit reading

cells.quote: Even though no group differences were observed early on, after two years children with dyslexia hypoactivated the left vOT and left IFG compared to both age and reading matched controls 42.
cells.note: The review reports a longitudinal group contrast after two years of formal education.

D.treatment: children at high risk of dyslexia

O.outcome_detail: hemispheric lateralization and right-hemisphere activity during reading

cells.quote: A magnetic source imaging study showed that 6-year olds with a high risk of dyslexia showed no leftward lateralization for reading tasks, while this pattern was clear in the control group. Lack of asymmetry reflected the increased activity of the right hemisphere, rather than left hemisphere hypoactivation, and was stable across kindergarten and first grade 55.
cells.note: The review interprets increased right-hemisphere engagement as part of an atypical or compensatory reading-network trajectory.

O.outcome_detail: fractional anisotropy of bilateral long arcuate fasciculus segments

cells.quote: Already prior to the reading onset, children with dyslexia showed lower FA of the bilateral long AF segments than typical readers
cells.note: The review reports a longitudinal neuroimaging comparison; no numerical effect size is provided.

O.outcome_detail: fractional anisotropy of the left arcuate fasciculus

cells.quote: Already prior to the reading onset, children with dyslexia showed lower FA of the bilateral long AF segments than typical readers, but after the reading onset differences in the left AF were canceled out
cells.note: The text describes the post-onset group difference as canceled out but does not report an equivalence test or adequate power.

O.outcome_detail: longitudinal N1 word-sensitivity trajectory

cells.quote: In a study following children from second to fifth grade, individuals with dyslexia did not show the expected reduction in N1 word sensitivity observed in typical readers 38. Group comparisons per time point showed that the N1 word sensitivity effect was reduced in children with dyslexia but this difference was no longer signiﬁcant in ﬁfth grade, where a trend for the opposite pattern was found.
cells.note: The review synthesizes a longitudinal ERP comparison; the direction varies across developmental time points.

O.outcome_detail: longitudinal LPC trajectory during audiovisual reading

cells.quote: The review entry reports ERP studies showing dyslexic readers lacked the expected reduction in N1 word sensitivity and showed reversed LPC trajectories after second grade, concluding "The results of these two studies are compatible with the notion of a protracted development of specialized responses in dyslexic readers."
cells.note: The provided study text describes the typical LPC trajectory—"The LPC amplitudes increased from kindergarten to first grade and subsequently decreased from the second to the fifth time point"—but the dyslexic-reader LPC comparison is not included in the supplied excerpt; the quote therefore uses the wiki entry as permitted.
